verses.text: At the time of the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, Joab led out the army, and wasted the country of the children of Ammon, and came and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem. Joab struck Rabbah, and overthrew it.

David took the crown of their king from off his head, and found it to weigh a talent of gold,  and there were precious stones in it. It was set on David’s head, and he brought very much plunder out of the city.

He brought out the people who were in it, and had them cut with saws, with iron picks, and with axes. David did so to all the cities of the children of Ammon. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After this, war arose at Gezer with the Philistines. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, of the sons of the giant; and they were subdued.
Again there was war with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam.
There was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had twenty-four fingers and toes, six on each hand, and six on each foot; and he also was born to the giant.
When he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David’s brother killed him.
These were born to the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants.

footnotes.content: David stays home while Joab wages war—a choice that cost him dearly. The comfort of the palace would lead him to Bathsheba's rooftop, and down a path of grave sin. Sometimes the hardest battles are the ones we don't rush toward, but face where He finds us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A talent of gold—about sixty pounds—crowning a king's head. The weight of power, the weight of conquest. Yet David's own head would know greater weight soon: the sorrows of his own house returning like that crown upon his brow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The harshness here stings. Even the victors among us need to remember: when we crush an enemy, we crush people bearing the image of God. The Lord's way leads to mercy before triumph, or triumph becomes its own ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sibbecai the Hushathite—a name almost forgotten. Yet he stood in the gap when a giant rose. How many faithful servants do their duty in obscurity, with no crowd watching, and the Lord sees them all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elhanan kills Lahmi, Goliath's brother. The same spirit that moved young David—that the Lord fights for His people—lives on in another man, another generation. The giants fall not by our strength, but by faith in the Lord's faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-four fingers and toes, twelve times the human measure. Malformation speaks to the brokenness that war and sin introduce into the world. Yet even the twisted creature born of strife falls to the hand of God's servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan, son of Shimea, David's own brother—he too wields God's strength. The same blood that fled to caves now stands firm against Philistine pride. Grace runs through families when it runs through a heart surrendered to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These giants fell by the hand of David and his servants. Looking back, we see how the Lord raises up leaders whose lives teach us: faithfulness to Him disarms the mightiest foes. Readers today hear an echo: the real giants we face—fear, pride, unforgiveness—fall the same way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
